name: Bioderma Sensibio H2O

lead: Sensibio H2O is a micellar water from the French company Bioderma, launched in 1991 and credited with popularising the product category worldwide.[2] Micelles are clusters of cleansing molecules that trap oil and makeup in their cores, so the liquid can lift them from skin with a cotton pad.[2]

People use it to cleanse and remove makeup gently, which supports a clear, calm-looking complexion. A 2021 questionnaire study examined its use for unpleasant skin sensations such as itching, tightness, tingling and burning.[1]

paras: It is applied to a cotton pad and wiped over face, eyes and lips as a first step or quick cleanse, usually without rinsing. Users pair it with a rinse-off cleanser or moisturiser depending on preference.
It is a cosmetic and generally mild, but any cleanser can irritate some skin; fragrance-free options and patch testing are common for reactive skin.

lead: Sensibio H2O is Bioderma's micellar water, a cleansing liquid for removing makeup and impurities from the face. Wikipedia credits its 1991 launch with helping micellar water spread worldwide.[1]

Micellar water is a dilute micellar solution in which molecules with oil-loving and water-loving ends form micelles that trap oily substances, letting the liquid lift makeup and excess oil. Typical formulas combine mild nonionic cleansing agents and moisturisers.[1]
A questionnaire study using a mobile app followed users of Sensibio H2O on days 0, 2, 14 and 28 to evaluate its effect on itching, tightness, tingling and burning sensations in sensitive skin.[2]

paras: Micelles trap oily substances in their cores, which lets the solution lift makeup and sebum from the skin.[1]
The French pharmaceutical company Bioderma launched Sensibio H2O in 1991; micellar skincare use is traced to 1913 and the product popularised the category worldwide.[1]

A 2021 study in Clinical, Cosmetic and Investigational Dermatology used app-based questionnaires at days 0, 2, 14 and 28 to evaluate Sensibio H2O for itching, tightness, tingling and burning sensations, citing a French survey in which about 30 percent of people report unpleasant skin sensations at least daily.[2]
